core: Federal, state, and local employment-law layers
supporting: EEOC coverage as an illustration of statute-specific coverage

claims.claim: Employment-law questions can involve federal, state, and local authorities; the DOL directs users to state labor offices and state-law resources covering topics such as wage, meal-period, payday, and child-labor rules.

For FLSA employee-versus-independent-contractor classification, the DOL's economic-reality inquiry asks whether the worker is economically dependent on the potential employer or is in business for themself, considering the totality of circumstances.
The DOL identifies factors concerning profit or loss, investments, permanence, control, integral work, and skill and initiative; no one factor determines status under the FLSA.
A title, a 1099, an independent-contractor agreement, or the time, mode, or location of payment or work does not alone determine FLSA classification.

At-will employment is commonly taught as an ongoing default relationship, but applicable federal or state law, constitutions, statutes, public policy, collective bargaining, and fixed-term agreements can limit a general statement about ending employment.
Federal employment-discrimination coverage can depend on the law and employer size, and an employer outside EEOC coverage may still be covered by state or local anti-discrimination law.
A workplace policy can communicate internal expectations or procedures but does not replace the statute, regulation, contract, or other legal authority governing a legal question.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Different legal regimes can use different worker definitions and coverage rules.
positions: The DOL Fact Sheet explains the FLSA economic-reality framework.
State, local, and other federal laws can supply additional or different rules.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson labels the FLSA test as statute-specific and avoids a universal classification conclusion.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft did not provide a source-verified, jurisdiction-aware account of worker classification, at-will limits, or legal layers.
